statement: In British Columbia in 2019, take-home testing by people who use drugs (strips from ten harm-reduction sites; 218 people returning 336 result sheets) compared with on-site testing of other samples by trained staff at the same sites in the same four months was associated with a similar share of fentanyl-positive results for opioid samples and a much larger share for stimulant samples. Opioids: 994 of 1105 take-home results positive (90.0%) against 591 of 663 on site (89.1%), a difference of 0.8 percentage points (95% CI −2.3 to 3.9) within the pre-set equivalence margin of ±5 points. Crystal methamphetamine: 73 of 265 (27.6%) against 5 of 97 (5.2%); cocaine: 16 of 93 (17.2%) against 1 of 92 (1.1%); the study was not powered for these. No sample was tested both at home and on site and nothing was confirmed in a laboratory, so these are shares of positive results, not accuracy; the authors nonetheless conclude that people can use the strips accurately with minimal training, and think the stimulant excess mostly reflects false positives from how samples were prepared at home, which was not tested (Klaire et al., 2022). Results were self-reported, about 6 in 10 sheets were filled in from memory at return (by the paper's Table 3; its text gives the reverse), the number of kits handed out and not returned is unknown, and similar shares near 90% can hide reading errors in both directions. A scoping review relays from other studies that 3% to almost 34% of people had difficulty interpreting results and that some believed the line's strength showed how strong the fentanyl was (Kutscher et al., 2024, second-hand; its figure of positives five times more frequent at home is this same study); a 2018 commentary relays a preliminary study in which 7 of 70 samples gave erroneous or invalid results (McGowan et al., 2018, second-hand); and in a laboratory study of a colour kit, two testers new to it misread known drugs in both directions (Murray et al., 2003). Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: When people tested their own drugs at home, the share of opioid samples showing fentanyl was about the same as when staff tested other samples on site (90 against 89 in 100). For crystal meth and cocaine, home tests showed fentanyl far more often (28 against 5 in 100 for meth), which the authors think were mostly false positives. No laboratory checked which results were right, and home and site tested different samples.
population: People using ten harm-reduction sites in British Columbia, Canada, April to July 2019, who took home fentanyl test strips and returned results (218 people, 336 sheets, 1680 strip results)
exposure: Fentanyl test strips used and read by the person wherever they chose to test, after brief peer training
comparator: On-site testing of other samples with the same strips by trained staff at the same sites in the same months (852 samples)
outcome: Share of fentanyl-positive strip results, by the drug the sample was expected to be
magnitude: Opioids: take-home 994/1105 (90.0%) against on-site 591/663 (89.1%); difference 0.8 points (95% CI −2.3 to 3.9), equivalent within ±5 (p = 0.00275). Crystal methamphetamine 73/265 (27.6%) against 5/97 (5.2%), difference 22.4 (14.8 to 30.1); cocaine 16/93 (17.2%) against 1/92 (1.1%), difference 16.1 (7.1 to 25.1). Second-hand: difficulty interpreting results 3% to almost 34% (Kutscher et al.); 7 of 70 erroneous or invalid results in a preliminary study (McGowan et al.).

evidence.locator: Methods › Statistical analysis, 1st paragraph; Results, 4th paragraph (p. 3); Table 2 (p. 4)
evidence.extracted: Pre-set equivalence margin ±5 percentage points. Opioids: 994 of 1105 take-home results positive (90.0%; the text gives 89.9%) against 591 of 663 on-site samples (89.1%); difference 0.81% (95% CI −2.3% to 3.9%; p = 0.00275 for equivalence; p = 0.59 for a difference in Table 2). The on-site group was 852 samples believed to be an opioid (663) or a stimulant (189) in isolation.

Crystal methamphetamine: 73 of 265 take-home results positive (27.6%) against 5 of 97 on site (5.2%), difference 22.4 (95% CI 14.8 to 30.1); cocaine: 16 of 93 (17.2%) against 1 of 92 (1.1%), difference 16.1 (7.1 to 25.1); the study was not sufficiently powered for the stimulant comparisons; 3.8% of strips gave an unclear or illegible reading.

evidence.locator: Results, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 3); Results, 6th paragraph; Table 3 (p. 4)
evidence.extracted: 336 result sheets (1680 results) were returned by 218 unique participants, for a 5 CAD honorarium, with no follow-up of kits not returned; Table 3 counts 206 sheets filled in from recall at return and 122 completed at the time of testing, while the text gives the reverse. Editors' calculation: 206 of 328 sheets (63%) from recall.

The authors infer from the similar opioid positivity that people who use drugs can use the strips accurately with minimal training; they judge the stimulant divergence more likely to reflect the testing method (false positives) than differently contaminated supplies, and name as limitations the assumption of no systematic difference between the samples tested by the two groups and the lack of a design in which the same sample is tested by the person and by an expert.
evidence.quote: PWUD can accurately use fentanyl test strips with minimal training

evidence.locator: Results › Feasibility of FTS Use › Ease of use, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Relays, without appraisal, that strips are often called easy but can be error prone: positive results occurred five times more frequently at home than at a drug-checking programme (reference 66); difficulty interpreting results ranged from 3% to almost 34% (references 38, 39 and 52); mistaken beliefs included that the intensity of the test shows the purity of fentanyl and that a negative fentanyl strip indicates xylazine. Editors' observation: the five-times figure matches Klaire et al. (2022), so it is the same study.
evidence.source_read: PDF PDFs/_Cross-cutting/Kutscher_2024_FTSScopingReview.pdf (PubMed Central author manuscript; AM p. = PDF page)

evidence.locator: Testing for fentanyl and fentanyl analogues, 3rd and 5th paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Second-hand: a preliminary study found that 7 of 70 drug samples tested returned erroneous or invalid results, after which Health Canada limited its endorsement of drug checking to supervised consumption sites; despite a lack of peer-reviewed evidence on self-testing, strips were being handed out and sold for home use at the time.

Two testers new to the colour kit, given only its labelling, misread known drugs in both directions with all three reagents: Novice A had two false negatives and one false positive, Novice B four false positives and no false negatives.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-I serious (study card): different samples and partly different people in the two groups, selective return of sheets with an honorarium, missing results, and self-reported, largely recalled readings.

indirectness.note: Shares of positive results stand in for accuracy; one province in 2019, one brand.

imprecision.note: The opioid interval treats 1105 results from 218 people as independent, and with plausible clustering the equivalence would no longer be shown (editors' calculation on the card); the stimulant comparisons were not powered.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision each rate it down, to the floor of very low. Rated as worded: agreement of shares of positive results between people testing at home and staff testing on site, not the accuracy of home testing, which no study read measured; whether home testing changes behaviour is a separate question. Status single study: the review's 'five times' figure is the same study, and Murray et al. concerns a colour kit in a laboratory and only qualifies.
